thread.title: Scientists gather at Lake Tahoe to address high-elevation climate change challenges
thread.title_full: Scientists gather at Lake Tahoe to address high-elevation climate change challenges

author: silver state times
title: Scientists gather at Lake Tahoe to address high-elevation climate change challenges
text:
High-elevation regions around the world, including Lake Tahoe, are facing increasing challenges due to a warming climate, with retreating glaciers and snowpacks leading to both flooding from rapid melt and future water scarcity. University scientists and global experts met in a workshop at the University of Nevada, Reno at Lake Tahoe from June 1-4 to collaboratively address these threats and explore solutions.
“High-elevation regions serve as critical water towers that sustain billions of people and countless ecosystems downstream,” said Baker Perry, Ph.D., professor of climatology and Nevada State Climatologist in the Department of Geography at the University of Nevada, Reno. “But we know very little about the past and current climates at the highest reaches of our own planet, leaving big gaps in our scientific understanding and ability to project future water resource availability in some of the most vulnerable places in the world.”
The workshop brought together leading high-elevation climate scientists from institutions based in mountain communities such as the Andes, Alps, Karakoram, and Himalaya Mountains. Industry representatives from Campbell Scientific and Kipp & Zonen also participated alongside early-career researchers studying high-elevation climate science topics. Participants used outdoor meetings on campus to connect with local landscapes while engaging in discussions.
“The Tahoe campus was the perfect place to host the workshop – with dedicated meeting, dining, and lodging space in close proximity,” said Perry. “Afternoon outings to the mountains and lake provided ample opportunities to enjoy the natural landscape and helped to facilitate deep discussion among participants.”
International collaborators worked together during sessions to identify major challenges for global high-elevation communities, find research gaps, and develop a framework for a peer-reviewed article addressing surprises, challenges, and solutions for mountain regions. The inclusion of researchers from low-income mountain countries allowed contemporary issues related to high-elevation warming—experienced firsthand by these communities—to be addressed directly.
“What is exciting about this workshop is its emphasis not only on advancing scientific understanding but also on building networks of collaboration, mentorship and shared data that will extend well beyond these few days together,” said Louisa Hope-Weeks, Ph.D., dean of the College of Science at the University. “The intentional inclusion of international partners, early-career scientists, and interdisciplinary perspectives speaks to the kind of community we must build to tackle complex global challenges.”
The event also focused on key scientific questions concerning Lake Tahoe’s region such as precipitation monitoring (rain versus snow), extreme events like atmospheric rivers, modeling weather patterns in mountains or snowpack dynamics. Julie Loisel stated: “The workshop brought together scientists with complementary expertise… Interdisciplinary experts don’t often get a chance to talk shop and exchange notes. This is extremely valuable because they all see different aspects of the issue.” Sponsors included foundations such as Heising-Simons Foundation; organizations like National Geographic Society; companies Campbell Scientific; Kipp & Zonen; RM Young; Furtenbach Adventures; as well as support from University.
